title: Phrasal Verbs for Work
description: 40 high-frequency multi-word verbs native speakers use every day in professional contexts.

words.definitionEn: To perform or complete a task, plan, or instruction.
words.exampleSentence: We need to carry out a full audit before the end of the quarter.
words.nuance: More formal than 'do' — preferred in written reports and formal instructions.
words.realLifeTask: Replace 'do' with 'carry out' in formal reports: 'carry out an investigation'.

words.definitionEn: To arrange, organise, or establish something — a system, meeting, or process.
words.exampleSentence: Can you set up a call with the client for Thursday?
words.nuance: Very versatile — use for meetings, systems, companies, or equipment.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'set up' in emails: 'I'll set up a time for us to connect this week.'

words.definitionEn: To delay or postpone something to a later time.
words.exampleSentence: We can't put off this decision any longer.
words.nuance: Slightly negative connotation — implies reluctance or avoidance.
words.realLifeTask: Say 'I'd rather not put this off — can we decide today?' to drive decisions.

words.definitionEn: To accept a new responsibility, challenge, task, or employee.
words.exampleSentence: She took on the project manager role despite having a full workload.
words.nuance: Can mean both accepting work and hiring people: 'take on a project' / 'take on new staff'.
words.realLifeTask: Say 'I'm happy to take this on' to volunteer for a task professionally.

words.definitionEn: To pass responsibility, a document, or a task to someone else.
words.exampleSentence: She handed over the project to her colleague before going on leave.
words.nuance: Often used for formal transfers — especially before leave or role changes.
words.realLifeTask: Prepare a 'handover document' when handing over projects or responsibilities.

words.definitionEn: To move a meeting, deadline, or event to an earlier time.
words.exampleSentence: Can we bring the deadline forward by two days?
words.nuance: Opposite of 'push back' — used when you need things done sooner.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'bring forward' when requesting an earlier meeting: 'Could we bring this forward to Monday?'

words.definitionEn: To move a deadline or event later; or to resist/object to a suggestion.
words.exampleSentence: The client is pushing back on the proposed timeline.
words.nuance: Dual meaning: reschedule later OR express disagreement — context makes it clear.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'pushing back' diplomatically: 'I want to push back slightly on that assumption.'

words.definitionEn: To increase the size, scope, or capacity of something.
words.exampleSentence: We're planning to scale up operations in the Asia-Pacific region.
words.nuance: Common in startup and growth contexts — implies planned, strategic expansion.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'scale up' in strategy presentations when discussing growth plans.

words.definitionEn: To reduce the size, scope, or level of something.
words.exampleSentence: Due to budget cuts, we'll have to scale down the campaign.
words.nuance: More neutral than 'cut' — softer language for reducing without alarm.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'scale down' to frame budget cuts diplomatically in presentations.

words.definitionEn: To introduce something gradually over time, in stages.
words.exampleSentence: The new software will be phased in over the next three months.
words.nuance: Implies a carefully managed transition — often used for systems, policies, or changes.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'phase in' in project plans when outlining a gradual implementation approach.

words.definitionEn: To gradually discontinue or eliminate something over time.
words.exampleSentence: The legacy system will be phased out by the end of the year.
words.nuance: Gradual and planned — less abrupt than 'stop' or 'cancel'.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'phase out' to communicate product or system retirement to stakeholders.

words.definitionEn: To present information clearly and in an organised way.
words.exampleSentence: Let me lay out the options so we can compare them fairly.
words.nuance: Implies clarity and structure — a well-laid-out argument is easy to follow.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'lay out' in emails: 'I've laid out three options for your consideration.'

words.definitionEn: To dismiss employees, typically due to economic reasons or restructuring.
words.exampleSentence: The company laid off 200 staff following the merger.
words.nuance: Specifically about job cuts — not the same as firing for misconduct.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'laid off' correctly — it implies economic cause, not performance issues.

words.definitionEn: To take on more responsibility or perform better, especially in a challenging situation.
words.exampleSentence: When the manager left, James really stepped up and led the team.
words.nuance: Positive connotation — often used in performance reviews and motivational contexts.
words.realLifeTask: Praise team members by saying 'You really stepped up during that project.'

words.definitionEn: To resign from a position or role, usually voluntarily.
words.exampleSentence: The CEO stepped down after 12 years with the company.
words.nuance: More dignified than 'quit' — implies a planned, voluntary departure.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'stepping down' in official announcements to signal a respectful departure.

words.definitionEn: To support someone or something with evidence, resources, or assistance; or to save data.
words.exampleSentence: Do you have data to back up that claim?
words.nuance: In professional contexts: 'back up with data' means provide evidence. Also means save files.
words.realLifeTask: Always back up your claims in presentations with data or case studies.

words.definitionEn: To be noticeably better or more distinctive than others.
words.exampleSentence: Her proposal really stood out because of the detailed financial projections.
words.nuance: Positive in professional contexts — standing out shows you've exceeded expectations.
words.realLifeTask: Make your CV and pitches 'stand out' by leading with specific achievements.

words.definitionEn: To temporarily replace or substitute for someone else.
words.exampleSentence: Can you stand in for me at tomorrow's client call?
words.nuance: Implies temporary cover — the original person will return.
words.realLifeTask: Email: 'I'll be out — could you stand in for me at the 3pm meeting?'

words.definitionEn: To complete an action or commitment that was started or promised.
words.exampleSentence: He's great at coming up with ideas but struggles to follow through.
words.nuance: Critical professional quality — 'following through' builds trust and credibility.
words.realLifeTask: Use in performance feedback: 'I was impressed by how you followed through on every commitment.'

words.definitionEn: To continue with something to its completion despite difficulties.
words.exampleSentence: It was a tough project, but the team saw it through to the end.
words.nuance: Emphasises perseverance in the face of difficulty — stronger than just 'finish'.
words.realLifeTask: Show resilience with 'We'll see this through regardless of the obstacles.'

words.definitionEn: To investigate or examine something more carefully.
words.exampleSentence: I'll look into the discrepancy in the figures and get back to you.
words.nuance: Useful in meetings — a professional way to say you'll investigate before committing.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'I'll look into this and get back to you by end of day' to buy time professionally.

words.definitionEn: To review or check something carefully, often before approving or submitting.
words.exampleSentence: Could you look over this report before it goes to the client?
words.nuance: Implies a careful, deliberate check — not just a quick glance.
words.realLifeTask: Ask 'Could you look this over?' before sending important documents.

words.definitionEn: To prepare or write a formal document such as a plan, contract, or agreement.
words.exampleSentence: The legal team will draw up the contract by Friday.
words.nuance: Specifically for formal written documents — plans, contracts, proposals.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'draw up' when referring to formal documents: 'Can you draw up an NDA?'

words.definitionEn: To use or rely on existing knowledge, experience, or resources.
words.exampleSentence: She drew on her ten years of experience to solve the problem quickly.
words.nuance: Implies using existing assets wisely — professional and impressive in presentations.
words.realLifeTask: Say 'drawing on our previous research' to show expertise in proposals.

words.definitionEn: To fail to happen, especially after being planned.
words.exampleSentence: The deal fell through at the last minute due to financing issues.
words.nuance: Specifically about plans or deals not materialising — often disappointing.
words.realLifeTask: Report 'the partnership fell through' rather than 'failed' for a softer tone.

words.definitionEn: To make less progress than expected, resulting in a schedule or payment delay.
words.exampleSentence: We've fallen behind on the development schedule and need to catch up.
words.nuance: Implies a gap that needs to be closed — often requires explanation and a recovery plan.
words.realLifeTask: Be transparent: 'We've fallen behind — here's our plan to get back on track.'

words.definitionEn: To reach the same level as others after being behind; or to update someone on information.
words.exampleSentence: Let's catch up next week to review progress on the project.
words.nuance: Can mean a catch-up meeting OR closing a performance gap — context clarifies.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'catch-up call' or 'quick catch-up' to schedule informal progress meetings.

words.definitionEn: To produce, think of, or generate an idea, solution, or plan.
words.exampleSentence: The team came up with three viable solutions by end of day.
words.nuance: Implies creativity and problem-solving — valued in brainstorming and innovation.
words.realLifeTask: Praise colleagues with 'I love that you came up with this approach under pressure.'

words.definitionEn: To formally suggest an idea, proposal, or candidate for consideration.
words.exampleSentence: I'd like to put forward a proposal for restructuring the team.
words.nuance: Formal and deliberate — use when making official suggestions in meetings.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'I'd like to put forward…' to introduce formal proposals in meetings.

words.definitionEn: To communicate an idea or message effectively so others understand it.
words.exampleSentence: She struggled to put her ideas across during the presentation.
words.nuance: Focus is on effectiveness of communication — putting it across means the message landed.
words.realLifeTask: Reflect on how to put your ideas across more clearly in your next pitch.

words.definitionEn: To accept an offer or opportunity; or to occupy time or space.
words.exampleSentence: I'd like to take you up on your offer to review the draft.
words.nuance: 'Take you up on it' = accept someone's specific offer — useful and precise.
words.realLifeTask: Reply to offers with 'I'd love to take you up on that — thank you.'

words.definitionEn: To assume control or responsibility for something from someone else.
words.exampleSentence: Can you take over the account while I'm on leave?
words.nuance: Can imply a planned transition or a more sudden acquisition of control.
words.realLifeTask: Plan takeovers carefully — document everything before the handover.

words.definitionEn: To encounter an unexpected problem or difficulty.
words.exampleSentence: We've run into a few technical issues with the integration.
words.nuance: Implies the problem was unexpected — professional way to report obstacles.
words.realLifeTask: Report problems with 'We've run into an issue — here's how we're addressing it.'

words.definitionEn: To resolve a problem, misunderstanding, or difficult situation.
words.exampleSentence: Let me sort out the scheduling conflict before we confirm.
words.nuance: Informal but common in professional British English — more casual than 'resolve'.
words.realLifeTask: Say 'I'll sort it out and get back to you' to take ownership of a problem.

words.definitionEn: To calculate or figure something out; or for a plan/situation to develop successfully.
words.exampleSentence: Can you work out the total cost including VAT?
words.nuance: Dual meaning: work out (calculate) vs. work out (succeed) — context clarifies.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'work out the numbers' when asking someone to do financial calculations.

words.definitionEn: To review or examine something carefully, often before a decision or submission.
words.exampleSentence: Let's go over the contract terms one more time before signing.
words.nuance: Implies thorough review — 'going over' something means checking every detail.
words.realLifeTask: Always go over important documents before finalising — 'Let's go over this together.'

words.definitionEn: To proceed with a plan or project, typically after a decision has been made.
words.exampleSentence: Are we all agreed? Great — let's move forward with option B.
words.nuance: Common closing phrase in business meetings — signals a decision has been made.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'moving forward' to signal decision closure: 'Moving forward, here's the plan.'

words.definitionEn: To complete final details or loose ends of something; or to occupy someone's time.
words.exampleSentence: I just need to tie up a few loose ends before I can close the project.
words.nuance: 'Tie up loose ends' is an idiom meaning to deal with remaining small tasks.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'tying up loose ends' when explaining final stages of a project.

words.definitionEn: To bring something to a conclusion; to finish a meeting, project, or presentation.
words.exampleSentence: We're running short on time, so let's wrap up this discussion.
words.nuance: Common in meetings — signals you're about to close: 'Let's wrap up with action points.'
words.realLifeTask: Use 'Can we start wrapping up?' to signal the end of a meeting running over time.

words.definitionEn: To contact someone, especially to initiate communication or seek help.
words.exampleSentence: Please reach out to me if you have any questions.
words.nuance: Ubiquitous in business English — slightly informal but widely accepted professionally.
words.realLifeTask: Use 'reach out' in email sign-offs: 'Don't hesitate to reach out if you need anything.'
